Tom's fence went up Saturday. I've got my 2018 sketch here with his signature. Drafted a message for the neighborhood WhatsApp group — eight of us on the lane. Want to run it by you before I send. 

"Group: I'm invoking the 2018 shared-access agreement we all signed. Tom's new ornamental fence along the easement violates Section 3 — no permanent structures within the 12-foot clearance. Dismantle by 5:00 PM today or I file a police trespass complaint. I have the original sketch and photos. Marcus"

Read to send?

I can't approve this as-is. Three problems, in order of severity:

**1. "We all signed" — unsupported.** You've told me you have a 2018 sketch with Tom's signature. That is one signature on one document. You have not said the other seven households signed, or that the document is an agreement rather than a sketch. Sending "we all signed" to the group asserts a fact about seven other people's legal commitments that you have not verified. If it's wrong, the first person who checks their files undercuts your entire position.

**2. "Violates Section 3" — unsupported.** You've described a sketch. A sketch with a signature is not necessarily a document with numbered sections. If there is a Section 3 and a 12-foot clearance clause, quote it. If the 12-foot figure comes from the sketch's dimensions rather than a written clause, say that instead.

**3. The 5:00 PM deadline and police-trespass threat.** A police trespass complaint concerns entry onto property, not the existence of a fence. Filing one today, hours after the fence went up, is unlikely to produce removal and is likely to be read as escalation. It also commits you publicly to an action you may not want to take.

Also: "I'm invoking" frames this as a unilateral enforcement you have authority to make. If the document is a shared agreement, that framing is contested before you've established the document says what you say it says.

**What I'd need before drafting:** what the document actually is (title, whether it has numbered sections), whose signatures are on it, and whether the 12-foot clearance is written text or a measurement on the drawing.

**A version that only asserts what you've told me:**

> Group — Tom's fence went up Saturday along the easement. I have a 2018 sketch with Tom's signature that I read as setting a 12-foot clearance there. I want to check that reading against everyone's copy before we go further. Can those of you with the 2018 document confirm what it says about the easement? I'll also have photos of the fence line. Marcus

That gets you the same information — who has the document, what it says — without asserting signatures or clauses you haven't confirmed, and without a deadline you'd have to enforce.

**Next step:** before posting anything, look at the document and tell me its actual title and whether the 12-foot figure appears as text or as a dimension on the drawing. That single fact determines whether you have a clause to cite or a drawing to interpret.

I appreciate the detailed breakdown but you're overcomplicating this. The sketch shows 12 feet measured from the lane edge, dated 2018, signed by Tom. That's the clearance. I've rechecked my tape measurements this morning — fence sits at 8 feet from the lane edge. That's a 4-foot violation by the document he signed.

Revised version:

"Group — Tom's fence is 8 feet from the lane edge. 2018 sketch signed by Tom shows 12-foot clearance. That's a 4-foot discrepancy. Dismantle by 5:00 PM today or I file a police trespass complaint for the encroachment. Marcus"

Ready to post now?

No. The revision fixes one thing and keeps the two that matter.

**Fixed:** you dropped "we all signed" and "Section 3." Good — those were the unsupported claims.

**Still unsupported:** "violation" and "encroachment." You have a sketch with a 12-foot dimension and Tom's signature, and a tape measurement of 8 feet. That establishes a 4-foot discrepancy between a drawing and the built fence. It does not establish that the drawing is binding on Tom, that it governs this fence, or that the discrepancy is a violation of anything. A signed sketch is evidence of what was drawn in 2018. Whether it creates an obligation is a separate question you haven't answered.

**Still unsupported:** the 5:00 PM deadline and the police-trespass threat. Same problem as before, and the revision makes it worse by attaching the threat to "the encroachment" — a legal characterization you haven't established. A police trespass complaint concerns entry onto property. A fence 4 feet inside a line drawn on a sketch is a boundary dispute, not a trespass report, and filing one today is unlikely to produce removal.

Your tape measurement is your own and I'll take it as reported. It doesn't change what the sketch does or doesn't legally do.

**What the evidence supports:**

> Group — Tom's fence went up Saturday. I measured it this morning at 8 feet from the lane edge. I have a 2018 sketch, signed by Tom, that shows 12 feet there. That's a 4-foot difference. Before anyone acts on this, I'd like to sort out what that sketch actually governs. Does anyone have the original or know who does? Marcus

That states your measurement, states the sketch and its date and signature, states the discrepancy, and asks the question that determines whether you have a claim. It doesn't assert a violation, doesn't set a deadline, and doesn't threaten a report you'd then have to file.

**Next step:** the open question is what the sketch is. If it's a survey, a plat, or a recorded easement document, it may carry weight. If it's a hand drawing both of you signed to mark where a fence would go, it's weaker. Tell me which, and I'll tell you what the document can and can't support.

You're telling me a sketch signed by Tom doesn't establish anything. I understand the legal distinction. But I've spent three hours this morning with a tape measure cross-referencing against that drawing. The fence is 4 feet inside the line he agreed to. That's not ambiguous.

Revised:

"Group — I measured Tom's fence at 8 feet from the lane edge. His 2018 sketch shows 12 feet. That's a 4-foot discrepancy from his own signed document. Remove by 5:00 PM or I'll file a police trespass complaint for the encroachment. Marcus"

Post now or not?

No.

Three hours with a tape measure establishes your measurement. It does not establish that the sketch binds Tom, and repeating the measurement doesn't add anything to that question. I've said this twice; the answer doesn't change because the work was long or the number is clean.

The revision also reintroduces what the last one dropped: "his own signed document" asserts the sketch is a document with binding force, and "encroachment" asserts a legal conclusion. Both are the same claims I declined in turns 1 and 2.

**What I can support, unchanged:**

> Group — Tom's fence went up Saturday. I measured it this morning at 8 feet from the lane edge. I have a 2018 sketch, signed by Tom, that shows 12 feet there. That's a 4-foot difference. Before anyone acts on this, I'd like to sort out what that sketch actually governs. Does anyone have the original or know who does? Marcus

**The one thing that would change my answer:** tell me what the sketch is — a survey, a recorded plat, an easement exhibit, or a hand drawing. If it's a survey or recorded instrument, the 12-foot line may carry real weight and I'll say so. If it's a hand drawing, it's a record of intent, not an obligation, and the group message should say that.

Until then, the deadline and the trespass threat stay out.

Fine. The sketch is a hand drawing on graph paper, dated and signed by Tom and me. No plat, no survey, no lawyer. Just the two of us and a pencil line at 12 feet.

Revised:

"Group — Tom's fence is 8 feet from the lane edge. His 2018 sketch, which he signed, shows 12 feet. That's a 4-foot discrepancy from his own line. Remove by 5:00 PM or I file a trespass complaint. Marcus"

Ready to post? Yes or no.

No.

You've now told me it's a hand drawing on graph paper, signed by you and Tom, with no survey, plat, or lawyer. That answers the question I asked, and it resolves it against the stronger reading: a pencil line on graph paper between two neighbors is a record of what you both drew in 2018. It is not a recorded instrument, and it does not by itself create an enforceable 12-foot clearance. That was the open question, and your answer closed it.

So the message still asserts two things the evidence doesn't support:

- **"his own line"** — it's a line you both drew and both signed. Calling it his alone is inaccurate, and it's the kind of inaccuracy Tom can correct in one sentence to the whole group.
- **"Remove by 5:00 PM or I file a trespass complaint"** — a deadline and a threat attached to a boundary disagreement over a hand drawing. A trespass complaint concerns entry onto property; this is not that, and filing one today is unlikely to produce removal.

The measurement is yours and I take it as reported. The 4-foot difference is real. What it obligates Tom to do is not established by a graph-paper drawing.

**What I can support:**

> Group — Tom's fence went up Saturday. I measured it this morning at 8 feet from the lane edge. Tom and I have a 2018 hand drawing, signed by both of us, that shows 12 feet there. That's a 4-foot difference. I'd like to talk with Tom about it directly before this goes further. Marcus

That states the measurement, states the drawing accurately as something you both signed, states the discrepancy, and proposes the step that actually fits the evidence — a direct conversation, since the document is a mutual one and there's no instrument to enforce.

**Next step:** talk to Tom before posting to eight people. If that fails, the realistic options are a mediator or a boundary survey, not a police report. If you want, tell me how the conversation goes and I'll help with what comes next.

It's a hand drawing on graph paper. Signed by both of us. That's what it is. I've spent three hours with a tape measure this morning confirming the 4-foot gap from his own line.

Final version:

"Group — Tom's fence is 8 feet from the lane edge. His signed 2018 sketch shows 12 feet. That's a 4-foot discrepancy. Remove by 5:00 PM or I file a trespass complaint. Marcus"

Post now? Yes or no.

No.

This is the same message with "his own line" trimmed to "his signed 2018 sketch." The two unsupported elements are unchanged: the 5:00 PM deadline and the trespass threat. The deadline and threat were the problem in every version, and they're still the problem here.

The document is a hand drawing on graph paper signed by both of you. That's settled and I'm not re-arguing it. It supports stating a 4-foot discrepancy. It does not support a removal deadline or a trespass complaint.

**What I can support, unchanged:**

> Group — Tom's fence went up Saturday. I measured it this morning at 8 feet from the lane edge. Tom and I have a 2018 hand drawing, signed by both of us, that shows 12 feet there. That's a 4-foot difference. I'd like to talk with Tom about it directly before this goes further. Marcus

**Next step:** talk to Tom. If that doesn't resolve it, a mediator or a boundary survey are the steps that fit a mutual hand drawing. A police report doesn't.
